tldr: For an omnidirectional autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) where obtaining an accurate hydrodynamic model is difficult, the authors developed a 6-DoF Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) scheme that learns and incorporates angular velocity dynamics errors using Gaussian Process (GP) regression. In real-world water tank experiments, it achieved attitude tracking accuracy superior to a field-proven PID controller while running in real-time at 25 Hz.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed GP-MPCC framework. A Gaussian Process (GP) learns model errors (residuals) from pre-collected data and adds them to the nominal model. In addition, predicted uncertainties are propagated using zero-order robust optimization (zoRO) to tighten constraints, enabling real-time contouring control.
overview:
Close-range inspection of underwater structures such as shipwrecks and pipelines requires high-precision position and attitude tracking so that targets can be observed from arbitrary angles. Holonomic (omnidirectional) AUVs, which can translate and rotate independently, are ideal for this task. However, accurately identifying complex hydrodynamic models underwater is extremely difficult. Model uncertainty significantly degrades the performance of Model Predictive Control (MPC).

To tackle this, the authors extended Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC)—which simultaneously optimizes "progress" along a geometric path and "contouring error" away from it—to all six degrees of freedom (6-DoF). Furthermore, they conceived a hybrid control scheme called "GP-MPCC," where the nominal model is roughly configured using simplified parameters from a different vehicle, and the mismatch (residual) with actual behavior is compensated from data using Gaussian Process (GP) regression. To keep the computational load low enough for real-time onboard deployment, they introduced a zero-order robust optimization (zoRO) scheme that propagates uncertainty outside the solver's iterative loop, securing a fast 25 Hz real-time control cycle.

The authors conducted validation using both a simulator and in-water tank experiments with the physical "MOLA" compact holonomic AUV developed by MBARI. The results revealed that learning all degrees of freedom blindly picks up sensor noise in the translational direction and actually degrades control performance. In contrast, learning and compensating only the physically meaningful "angular velocity (rotational) components" dramatically improves tracking performance. Compared to a high-precision PID controller refined in the field for years, the proposed method reduced attitude errors by up to 47% and successfully completed a 3D spiral inspection maneuver that the PID controller could not follow without failing.
contributions: Deployed a fully nonlinear 6-DoF Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) capable of independently tracking position and attitude on an actual holonomic AUV in real-time (25 Hz) for the first time.
Compensated nominal model errors via Gaussian Process (GP) regression and realized uncertainty-aware constraint tightening with low computational cost using zero-order robust optimization (zoRO).
Demonstrated through simulation ablation studies that learning all degrees of freedom degrades performance due to noise, proving that focusing the learning on rotational dynamics is critical.

Validated superior tracking performance in tank experiments on survey patterns and challenging spiral inspection trajectories compared to a nominal MPCC and a field-proven PID controller tuned over years of field deployment.

sections.heading: Freely Viewing Underwater Structures: The Challenge of Full-DoF Control
sections.summary: Small holonomic AUVs that can control camera viewpoints independently of their translation direction are valuable for precise underwater inspection. However, identifying underwater dynamics is exceptionally difficult, creating a major obstacle for MPC. This work overcomes this challenge by proposing a 6-DoF MPCC that compensates for model errors using Gaussian Processes.
sections.details:
Close-range inspection and survey of underwater infrastructure such as shipwrecks, pipelines, and underwater mines require advanced maneuvering, such as circling intricately around structures while keeping a camera pointed steadily at targets. While torpedo-shaped cruising AUVs are suited for wide-area searches, they lack agility. On the other hand, tethered Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs) require support vessels and skilled operations crews, driving up operational costs significantly.

This has brought compact holonomic (omnidirectional) AUVs into the spotlight, such as the "MOLA AUV" developed by MBARI. Through clever thruster arrangements, these vehicles can control their translation direction and body orientation (attitude) completely independently. However, moving safely near structures requires an advanced controller capable of tracking complex trajectories while strictly respecting state and thruster constraints. Model Predictive Control (MPC) is best suited for these requirements, but MPC relies heavily on an "accurate dynamics model." Underwater hydrodynamic parameters (such as added mass and hydrodynamic drag) are highly nonlinear, strongly coupled, and change with payload alterations or environments, making perfect identification nearly impossible.

Recent studies have explored using machine learning to compensate for model errors, but they were either restricted to 4-DoF or limited to simulation validation. This work establishes a nonlinear 6-DoF Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) that tracks position and attitude independently, corrects model residuals using Gaussian Processes (GP), and validates the entire pipeline seamlessly all the way through in-water tank experiments on the physical "MOLA AUV."

sections.heading: Evolution of Prior Work: From 3-DoF to 6-DoF, and On to Contouring Control
sections.summary: Due to computational limits, MPC for underwater robots has often been simplified to 3 or 4 degrees of freedom, and 6-DoF studies remained mostly in simulation. Furthermore, prior tracking was largely time-parameterized. This work is the first to deploy contouring control (MPCC), which optimizes geometric progress itself, to a physical 6-DoF underwater vehicle.
sections.details:
MPC applications for underwater vehicles have been actively researched in recent years, but most have been restricted to 3-DoF planar motion: surge, sway, and yaw. While reducing model order accelerates computation, inspecting structures from arbitrary angles requires active tilt control of roll and pitch in addition to depth (heave). While some MPC studies have considered all 6 degrees of freedom, the vast majority were confined to simulations.

Experimental validations on physical vehicles have been reported for partial-DoF control of AUVs with manipulators, position/velocity control of holonomic AUVs, and docking maneuvers. However, all of these were time-parameterized trajectory tracking or waypoint tracking methods that specify "reaching a given coordinate at a given time." In contrast, the "Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC)" adopted here defines deviations from a geometric path (contouring error and lag error) and treats the progress rate along the path as an optimization decision variable. While MPCC has demonstrated great success in time-optimal driving of autonomous cars and drones, no previous study has deployed it to a full 6-DoF underwater robot.

Regarding learning-based model error compensation, previous studies either assumed self-righting ROV properties to reduce the model to 4-DoF, or learned only hydrodynamic damping terms in simulation. This paper expands upon those prior frameworks, introducing general residual learning without restricting it to specific physical terms, and elevates it to real-time execution on a physical robot.

sections.heading: Problem Formulation and Vehicle Dynamics: Starting Intentionally from an Imperfect Model
sections.summary: The system consists of a first-principles nominal model, unknown residuals, and process noise. The vehicle equations of motion use standard Fossen dynamics, with attitude represented by quaternions to prevent singularities. Intentionally, hydrodynamic coefficients from a different vehicle are reused for the nominal model, setting up the problem so learning compensates for modeling errors.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation
The target system is a discrete-time nonlinear system composed of a known first-principles nominal model $\bm{f}$, an unknown residual function $\bm{g}$ representing unmodeled dynamics and parameter mismatches, and white process noise $\bm{w}$. The MPC solves an optimal control problem across a finite prediction horizon based on this model. The unknown residual $\bm{g}$ is extracted as data samples by subtracting the nominal model prediction from consecutive state observations.

### III-B Notation
The state vector is denoted by $\bm{x}$ and the control input by $\bm{u}$. The weighted squared norm is defined as $\|\bm{a}\|_{\bm{W}}^2 = \bm{a}^\mathrm{T}\bm{W}\bm{a}$. Steps along the prediction horizon are denoted by $k$.

### III-C AUV Equations of Motion
The vehicle's equations of motion adopt Fossen's standard marine engineering formulation. It is described by a mass matrix $\bm{M}$ including rigid-body and added mass, a Coriolis matrix $\bm{C}$, a hydrodynamic damping matrix $\bm{D}$, a gravity/buoyancy vector $\bm{g}$, and external forces $\bm{\tau}$ such as thruster inputs. The coordinate frame is Forward-Right-Down (with positive depth $z$). To avoid Euler angle singularities (gimbal lock), attitude is represented using unit quaternions $\bm{q}$.

Here lies a very practical and intriguing design decision: the accurate hydrodynamic parameters of the target MOLA AUV were not identified beforehand. Instead, the authors directly reused parameters from the open-source "BlueROV2", which has a relatively similar hull shape, as the nominal model $\bm{f}$. In other words, they began with the premise that "a certain level of modeling error already exists from the start," adopting an approach that bridges the gap via downstream learning.

sections.heading: Balancing Geometric Path and Viewpoint: Mathematics of 6-DoF MPCC
sections.summary: To optimize progress along a geometric path rather than following a strict time trajectory, position error is decomposed into tangential path error (lag error) and normal plane error (contouring error) and penalized. Leveraging holonomic capabilities, quaternion-based attitude tracking error is independently added to the cost function, enabling smooth 3D inspection paths.
sections.details:
### IV-A Decomposition of Contouring and Lag Errors
Specifying "where the vehicle should be at what second," as done in traditional MPC, often leads to aggressive control inputs whenever small disturbances cause minor delays. In MPCC, the arc-length parameter $\theta$ along the geometric path is treated as a virtual state variable (decision variable). The position error $\bm{e}(\theta_k)$ between the vehicle's current position $\bm{p}_k$ and the path coordinate $\bm{p}(\theta_k)$ is orthogonally decomposed into "lag error $e^l$", which is the projection onto the path tangent vector $\bm{t}(\theta_k)$, and "contouring error $\bm{e}^c$" within the normal plane perpendicular to the direction of travel. This allows deviation from the path and falling behind progress to be weighted and penalized independently.

### IV-B Optimal Control Problem Formulation
The overall cost function includes penalties on contouring and lag errors, a reward term for moving along the path (formulated as a squared error against a virtual target progress velocity to maintain convexity), input rate regularization on thruster commands $\Delta \bm{u}$, and progress acceleration/deceleration $\Delta v_\theta$. As the key strength of this method, an "attitude error term" is introduced to exploit holonomic capabilities. Rotational errors derived from the quaternion product between target and current attitudes are penalized, and inter-step attitude changes $\Delta \bm{q}_k$ are also penalized to prevent abrupt angular velocity changes. In addition, a nonlinear state constraint keeps the vehicle inside a cylinder of radius $r$ centered on the reference path.

### IV-C Reference Trajectory Generation
The inspection path is generated from spatial position and attitude waypoints. Position coordinates are smoothly joined using cubic splines, and the arc length $\theta$ is computed at each point. Attitude references are interpolated along the same arc-length parameter using Spherical Linear Interpolation (SLERP) between waypoints. This produces a smooth reference trajectory where positional progress and the intended viewing direction remain perfectly synchronized.

With respect to the red reference path, the vehicle position error is decomposed into a tangential lag error $e^l$ and a normal-plane contouring error $e^c$.

sections.heading: Integrating Gaussian Processes: Computational Tricks to Run at 25 Hz with Uncertainty
sections.summary: Unknown residual dynamics are modeled using Gaussian Processes (GPs), embedding not only predictive means but also variances (uncertainty) into the controller. By using "zero-order robust optimization (zoRO)" to propagate covariance outside the optimization loop, fast real-time control at 25 Hz is achieved.
sections.details:
### V-A Gaussian Process (GP) Regression
Taking collected state-input pairs $\bm{z} = [\bm{x}^\mathrm{T}, \bm{u}^\mathrm{T}]^\mathrm{T}$ as inputs, a Gaussian Process is trained with the target $\bm{y}$ being the acceleration mismatch unexplained by the nominal model. A squared exponential kernel with Automatic Relevance Determination (ARD) is used. The advantage of a GP is that it provides both the predictive mean $\mu^g$ and the uncertainty (variance $\Sigma^g$) in regions with scarce training data.

### V-B Acceleration via Zero-Order Robust Optimization
When embedding the learned GP into MPC, in addition to propagating the mean dynamics along the prediction horizon, state constraints are tightened according to uncertainty ("constraint tightening"). This automatically maintains safety margins when the model is uncertain.

However, including the covariance propagation equations directly into the decision variables of a Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) solver causes a computational explosion, making real-time solving on a real vehicle impossible. To circumvent this, the authors adopted an ingenious strategy called "zero-order robust optimization (zoRO)." Based on the optimal trajectory from the previous control step, the covariance is propagated linearly *outside* the SQP iteration loop, and the constraint tightening margin $\beta$ is precomputed as a fixed value. Consequently, the optimization problem solved online retains the exact same structure as a standard nominal MPC. Using the Real-Time Iteration (RTI, one SQP iteration per step) scheme provided by acados, a stable 25 Hz control rate is achieved with execution times of just a few milliseconds.

sections.heading: Experimental Setup: What Should We Actually Learn as a Residual?
sections.summary: Tank experiments were carried out linking the open-source underwater simulator "Stonefish" and the physical "MOLA AUV" under identical software architectures. Residual analysis revealed that translational velocity residuals were buried in noise, while angular velocity residuals showed clear physical structure, proving that selective learning dictates performance.
sections.details:
### VI-A Residual Learning in Practice and "Selecting What to Learn"
Independent GP models were trained for the six velocity components (surge, sway, heave, roll, pitch, yaw). Training data was collected through open-loop excitation that stimulated each axis individually and in combination, then uniformly downsampled to 100 points to keep inference latency within the real-time budget.

Here, an illuminating discovery was made. When visualizing residual data from the real vehicle, linear velocity residuals such as forward surge showed almost no patterns and were dominated by measurement noise. In contrast, rotational residuals such as roll rate exhibited clear physical structure that the GP captured effectively. Incorporating noisy linear residuals into the MPC injects unnecessary noise into the controller and degrades performance. Therefore, the authors decided to compensate only for rotational residuals (angular velocity components) in subsequent experiments.

### VI-B Evaluation Metrics
To evaluate path following, the closest point on the reference spline curve was identified for the vehicle's position at each time step. Position error and attitude rotation error (quaternion RMSE) at that point were computed. In addition, total control effort (accumulated absolute commanded thrust) was recorded as an energy metric.

### VI-C & VI-D Scenarios and System Architecture
Validation took place in the "Stonefish" physics simulator and in a $13\times 9\times 10\,\mathrm{m}$ saltwater test tank using MBARI's physical "MOLA AUV." The vehicle is equipped with an IMU, pressure sensor, and Doppler Velocity Log (DVL), running an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) on an onboard NVIDIA Orin NX for state estimation. Baselines included the nominal MPCC (nom), GP-MPCC compensating rotational residuals (gp-pqr), GP-MPCC compensating all residuals (gp-full), and a field-proven PID controller tuned meticulously over years of operations. Two tasks were evaluated: a "lawnmower pattern" scanning a wide area at fixed heading, and a challenging "inspection spiral trajectory" ascending while rotating and adjusting pitch to constantly gaze at a central target.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion: The Pitfall of Full-DoF Learning and Real-World Superiority
sections.summary: Simulation ablations showed that learning all DoFs halved performance, whereas compensating only angular velocities significantly improved attitude accuracy. In physical tank experiments, GP-MPCC reduced attitude error by 47% compared to the expertly tuned PID and accurately traced a 3D spiral inspection trajectory that PID could not execute.
sections.details:
### VII-A Simulation Results
In the lawnmower pattern ablation, "gp-pqr" (learning only rotational residuals) reduced attitude RMSE by 32% from $0.81^\circ$ to $0.55^\circ$ relative to the nominal MPCC (nom), while maintaining identical position error (0.06 m) and control effort. In contrast, "gp-full" (learning all residuals) roughly doubled both position and attitude errors and caused erratic oscillations with surging control energy. This provided clear evidence that learning noisy linear velocities has an adverse effect.

On the more dynamic "inspection spiral trajectory," differences grew even larger. In nominal MPCC, unmodeled rotational dynamics proved fatal: attitude RMSE fluctuated widely between $8^\circ$ and $48^\circ$ (mean $31^\circ$), failing to keep the target in view. By comparison, "gp-pqr" tracked with an attitude RMSE of just $4.5^\circ$, improved position RMSE from 0.048 m to 0.043 m, and lowered energy consumption by 6%.

### VII-B Physical Tank Experiment Results
In the physical lawnmower experiment, nominal MPCC matched the PID controller's position accuracy (0.033 m) while reducing attitude RMSE from $4.5^\circ$ to $3.2^\circ$. Introducing GP-MPCC with rotational residual compensation further brought attitude RMSE down to $2.4^\circ$. This represents a substantial 47% error reduction over the proven PID and a 25% reduction over nominal MPCC. Control energy increased by 28% compared to nominal MPCC, reflecting more agile thruster firings to maintain attitude (which can be mitigated by weight tuning).

The decisive contrast appeared during the physical "inspection spiral trajectory." The conventional PID controller, which tracks sequential waypoints by controlling each axis independently, could not handle multi-DoF dynamic coupling. It degraded into jerky, stepped motions and failed completely to execute the smooth intended spiral inspection. In contrast, the proposed MPCC traced the spline-interpolated path and viewing direction flawlessly on the real vehicle.

### VII-C Discussion
These findings offer a crucial practical lesson: when applying learning-based control to underwater robots, rather than "dumping everything onto a learner," filtering down to physically meaningful residuals (here, rotational dynamics) based on domain knowledge is essential for success. Moreover, compared to PID controllers requiring artisanal tuning over years of field deployments, MPCC delivered equal or superior performance with far less tuning effort, while offering the clear practical advantage of explicitly enforcing state and input constraints.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Outlook: Toward the Future of Autonomous Inspection
sections.summary: This study presented a 6-DoF MPCC augmented by Gaussian Processes for holonomic AUVs, verifying its effectiveness in simulation and water tank experiments. Future work points to online sequential learning, incorporating navigation uncertainty, and expanding to obstacle avoidance.
sections.details:
This paper developed a 6-DoF nonlinear MPCC for holonomic AUVs capable of fully independent position and attitude tracking, introducing the GP-MPCC framework that remedies nominal model deficits through Gaussian Process regression. Through simulations and tank trials, the authors proved the importance of selective residual learning, demonstrating that compensating for rotational dynamics cuts attitude errors of a field-proven PID controller in half. They also showed that complex 3D inspection maneuvers impossible for PID can be executed reliably with less tuning effort.

Outlined directions for future work include:
- Introducing online sequential learning to adapt to dynamic changes over long missions (such as buoyancy foam water absorption or thruster aging) and active learning to efficiently cover the state space.
- Directly incorporating underwater navigation uncertainty into the GP-MPCC uncertainty propagation scheme to handle imperfect state estimation.
- Refining constraint tightening techniques to ensure robust execution during ultra-close inspection of fragile underwater assets.
- Expanding MPCC's flexible constraint handling to obstacle avoidance and seabed terrain following.

takeaways: "Learning every degree of freedom" does not guarantee improvement: including translational velocities dominated by sensor noise destabilizes the closed-loop system, making domain knowledge essential to target axes with clear physical structure (rotational dynamics).

Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) is an ideal match for holonomic AUVs: optimizing spatial path progress and camera orientation (quaternion attitude) independently enables smooth execution of complex inspection trajectories that orbit targets while gazing inward.

Integrating computationally intensive GPs with MPC can run at 25 Hz on hardware via zoRO (zero-order robust optimization): propagating covariance outside the solver iteration loop maintains the exact same solver structure as nominal MPC.

Compared to meticulously tuned PID controllers, MPCC drastically reduces tuning overhead while accurately handling coupled multi-DoF motion and explicitly enforcing thruster and workspace constraints.
limitations: Because learning is based on offline data, the system cannot adapt on the fly to runtime dynamic changes, such as buoyancy shifts during long dives, varying ocean currents, or added payloads (online learning remains future work).

The water tank experiments assumed high-precision sensor fusion; the severe acoustic blackout periods and DVL drift errors inherent in open-ocean underwater state estimation were not explicitly handled.

While compensating rotational residuals improved attitude accuracy significantly, control inputs became more aggressive, causing an increase in energy consumption (which requires careful tuning of input rate weights).
